cases.interviewerQuestion: You went with bearer-token auth specifically because extensions can't share cookies with the main app's domain — what did that decision cascade into on the backend in terms of session handling or security review, especially across 30+ route handlers?
cases.tonyRaw: Once cookies were off the table, every one of those 30+ route handlers had to authenticate off the bearer token instead of inheriting session state for free, so I had to make sure token validation was consistent everywhere rather than bolted on per-route as I went. That's the real risk with an approach like this — it's easy to get the happy path working on a handful of routes and then have someone add route 31 without the same checks. Since I owned the whole surface solo, I was able to keep that consistent rather than relying on a review process to catch drift, but it also meant the burden of getting it right across all of them sat entirely on me. The Liveblocks passthrough and CRUD proxying added another wrinkle since those needed the same token trust extended into the real-time layer, not just standard REST calls.

cases.interviewerQuestion: What was the tell that pushed you toward splitting the store into three layers—was there a specific stale-state bug that made the undifferentiated approach untenable, or did the pain build up gradually across features?
cases.tonyRaw: It built up gradually rather than one dramatic bug — the pattern was that stale-state and unnecessary re-render issues kept showing up in different parts of the app, and each time the root cause traced back to treating fundamentally different kinds of state as if they belonged in the same store. Real-time collaborative state, server-persisted state, and local UI state have different consistency guarantees and different invalidation rules, and mixing them meant a change in one would trigger re-renders or staleness in another for no good reason. Once I saw that pattern repeat across a few features, splitting into Liveblocks for the collaborative layer, TanStack Query for server state, and a reducer for local UI state was the fix — each layer got the invalidation and update semantics it actually needed instead of one undifferentiated store trying to serve all three.

cases.interviewerQuestion: Learning Spanner and Dataflow on the fly while co-leading the migration, what did the staged approach actually look like — how did you decide where to cut the boundaries between stages, and what did the regression testing need to catch before you'd trust a stage as done?
cases.tonyRaw: I co-led our SQL to Google Cloud Spanner migration, learning Spanner and Cloud Dataflow alongside the rest of the team as we drove a $500K per year infrastructure cost reduction. We cut stage boundaries around data domains that had clear ownership and limited cross-references to other tables still on SQL, since Spanner's consistency model and indexing behave differently enough that mixing partially-migrated and legacy data in one stage was asking for silent corruption. Each stage's regression testing had to cover both correctness of the migrated data itself, comparing row-level output between old and new systems, and behavior under actual query load, because Spanner's performance characteristics under concurrent access were the part neither of us had real intuition for yet. A stage wasn't done until we'd run production-shaped traffic against it and the diffs came back clean, not just when the Dataflow job completed without errors.

cases.interviewerQuestion: You had to integrate AI-generated content into ProseMirror's typed node model while supporting two concurrent editor versions at once. What made that dual-version support so tricky, and did the AI feature end up shaping the state-management design in ways you didn't anticipate?
cases.tonyRaw: I co-led a team of 3 to 4 engineers on that feature, and I personally designed the state-management layer that integrated AI output into ProseMirror's typed node document model. The dual-version piece was tricky because AI-generated content isn't just text you insert, it has to resolve into valid nodes under whatever schema and transaction rules the editor version in front of it actually enforces, and those two versions didn't treat document structure identically. So the design couldn't assume a single shape coming out of the AI call — it had to normalize into an intermediate representation before it ever touched ProseMirror's transaction pipeline, which was more upfront abstraction than we would have needed for a single-version editor. That constraint ended up shaping the whole approach more than I expected going in — the state layer became less about wiring AI output into the doc and more about isolating the editor from the AI entirely.

The duplication crept in because status-checking logic ended up written separately in a couple of places that needed to know bot state: the UI polling loop and the transcript-piping path, each written against its own assumptions about what "ready" meant. cases.interviewerQuestion: How did you go about validating calculation accuracy for those high-volume trader accounts—what did the comparison process between the old TypeORM implementation and the new port actually look like?
cases.tonyRaw: I worked on porting our trade metric computation from a TypeORM-based implementation into our new GraphQL API architecture, validating calculation accuracy with stakeholders along the way. The risk in a port like this isn't usually the happy path, it's edge cases in high-volume accounts where small rounding or aggregation differences compound across a lot of trades. So the validation was really about running the old and new computations against the same accounts and treating any divergence as a signal to dig into, rather than assuming the port was correct just because it compiled. Stakeholders were involved specifically because they knew what the numbers were supposed to look like for those accounts, which caught discrepancies I wouldn't have flagged on my own.

cases.interviewerQuestion: You spent nine months iterating on the delay and timing for the debounced autosave — what was actually going wrong at the settings you tried before you landed on ones that worked, and how could you tell?
cases.tonyRaw: The core tension was between saving too aggressively and saving too late. When the delay was too short, we'd fire saves while someone was still mid-edit, which meant unnecessary writes and dirty-state flags flapping on and off in a way that made the UI feel noisy. When it was too long, the dirty-state tracking would show unsaved changes sitting there for an uncomfortably long window, so if something went wrong you had a real risk of losing meaningful work. I could tell which failure mode I was in by watching how the dirty flag behaved under normal editing patterns rather than guessing at a number — thrashing meant too aggressive, a visibly stale dirty indicator meant too conservative. It took nine months because the right setting depended on real usage patterns in the artifact editor, not something you could derive analytically up front.

cases.interviewerQuestion: What tradeoffs came up while shaping the data model, and how much of that design held up once you started wiring it into the GraphQL layer?
cases.tonyRaw: I was part of a team that built the Trader Public Profile platform — I contributed to the data model design and helped build the GraphQL API layer and React UI, but this wasn't a feature I owned end to end, so I can speak to the parts I was in the room for rather than the whole arc. The main tension in the data model was how much to shape it around what the profile UI needed to render versus keeping it generic enough that other consumers of the same trader data wouldn't have to work around our choices. Wiring it into GraphQL is usually where those assumptions get tested, since the resolver layer exposes any place you modeled for one screen instead of the underlying entity.
